entities.label: Place
entities.summary:
Kiribati (pronounced 'Kiri-bas') is an island nation in the central Pacific Ocean, comprising 33 coral atolls and reef islands spanning over 3.5 million km² of ocean. With 120,000 people spread across the Phoenix Islands, Line Islands, and Gilbert Islands, Kiribati straddles the equator and the International Date Line — one of the most geographically dispersed nations on Earth.

Kiribati was colonized by Britain (as the Gilbert and Ellice Islands Colony) in the 19th century and gained independence in 1979. The Gilbert Islands were a significant theater of World War II — the Battle of Tarawa (November 1943) was one of the bloodiest US Marine landings of the Pacific campaign, capturing a heavily fortified Japanese airbase in 76 hours at the cost of 1,000 US and 4,500 Japanese dead. The brutality of Tarawa shocked the American public and led to significant reforms in amphibious assault tactics.

Kiribati faces an existential threat from climate change. At an average elevation of 2 meters above sea level, it is among the most vulnerable nations in the world to rising seas. The government has purchased land in Fiji as a potential refuge for climate refugees and has been the most prominent small island voice in international climate negotiations. If sea level rise continues at current projections, Kiribati's inhabited islands may become uninhabitable by the end of the 21st century — making it a potential pioneer case of the first climate-driven loss of a nation-state.
